The National Assembly's meeting today commenced at 1:31 PM under the chairmanship of the Honorable Chairperson, Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, the proceedings of today's National Assembly meeting (1:31 PM) are commencing. Honorable members, names have been received to speak during the zero hour. I will provide time for the honorable members to speak.
First, Honorable Member Khamma Bahadur Khati.
Honorable Mr. Khamma Bahadur Khati (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, I am going to speak about the incident of October 10th midnight. For what reasons was former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana detained for more than 12 hours without conditions? It is said he was kept in a safe place due to security threats; what does this mean? Who posed a threat to him? Why was the National Human Rights Commission team not allowed to meet him? Is this a government according to the constitution or not? If it is, does this government have to abide by the constitution and laws or not? Article 20 of the constitution states that the right to justice requires informing the reason for arrest and detention; this has been violated. The right to freedom, the right to human rights have been curtailed. Section 9 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 2074, has been directly violated. Through you, Honorable Chairperson, I request the government or the Home Minister to be directed to provide a clear answer in the parliament regarding this. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Chandra Bahadur KC.
Honorable Mr. Chandra Bahadur KC (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, as per the schedule, this session is ending tomorrow. This issue has been raised repeatedly regarding the Prime Minister's statement about the border. He neither came to this parliament to respond nor was his statement removed from the parliamentary record. Therefore, I demand that this statement be removed from the parliamentary record as soon as possible. Simultaneously, I demand that the construction of bridges and roads and the maintenance and reconstruction of roads under the Kaligandaki Corridor be carried out as soon as possible. The bridge in Dodhara Chandani, Kanchanpur, which is damaged and has collapsed, should be repaired immediately using a Bailey bridge or some other means, keeping in mind that Bada Dashain, Chhath, and Diwali are approaching. Thank you. Jai Nepal.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Dharmendra Paswan.
Honorable Mr. Dharmendra Paswan (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, the embankments on both sides of the Lal Bakaiya River in wards 1, 2, 3, and 4 of Paroha Municipality, Rautahat, have become two to four feet lower. Although this has been raised in the house repeatedly, why has the government not taken interest? If the embankment breaks, five hundred households will be destroyed. Therefore, I demand that the government rebuild the embankment to its original height. Thank you. Jai Nepal.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Mahanta Thakur.
Honorable Mr. Mahanta Thakur (Loktantrik Samajwadi Party Nepal):- Honorable Chairperson, the midnight arrest of the former Chief Justice has raised many ethical questions. Does a destroyed monarchy wish to be revived again? This question has arisen, and if so, they should be cremated at the Aryaghat this time, ensuring they do not return. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Meenasingh Rakhala.
Honorable Mr. Meenasingh Rakhala (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, how long will we watch the poor condition of Karnali's roads? Narrow roads, still unpaved in many places, muddy and risky roads even with normal rainfall, lack of bridges in some places; for this reason, the citizens of Karnali have to travel with the risk of their lives, not just travel. Some have lost their lives in road accidents, and some are forced to live as lifelong disabled. The future of the citizens and children in the affected families is dark. My question to the federal government is, instead of providing relief and condolences after an accident, when will safe roads be built to prevent accidents? Will progress be shown on paper by allocating budgets in the name of roads, or will roads be built where citizens can travel safely? Quality and safe road infrastructure is needed in Karnali; when will the government pay attention? Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri.
Honorable Mr. Ram Kumari Jhankri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, many books have been written in the world about how fascism or dictatorship comes. It seems we are also being subjected to such practices now. Just yesterday, former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana was arrested at night. But the government has no answer, making it difficult even to save face; for what reason was he arrested? There is no basis, no reason, no accountability. What does this mean? Is it a way to indirectly attack the judiciary and the legislature, understanding that the executive has unlimited power among the three branches of the state? Through you, Honorable Chairperson, I want to question this government, the Prime Minister, and the Home Minister, holding them accountable, and I want to ask this in the upcoming session. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Rekha Kumari Jha.
Honorable Ms. Rekha Kumari Jha (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, this is a serious and sensitive issue. During natural disasters like floods, landslides, and inundation that occur during the monsoon in Nepal, there is widespread public grievance and concern about the suffering faced by citizens and the government's role. In such challenging times, the market price of cooking gas, rice, lentils, and sugar, which citizens need daily, has skyrocketed. I want to draw the government's attention, through you, Chairperson, to monitor those involved in black marketing and take legal action against such individuals. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Roshi Mechhe.
Honorable Mr. Roshi Mechhe (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, in the past, we used to keep our savings in a "khutruke" (piggy bank), and then store it in a drawer. In recent times, with the progression of time and development, we have moved towards paperless or faceless technology. As we move in that direction, the situation has arisen where we all have to keep our money in banks and start saving in banks. Then, we have all started transacting through mobile banking. However, while transacting through mobile banking, it is observed that money has been stolen or hacked from many personal accounts through mobile banking. Therefore, is it not the responsibility of the state to protect the property of citizens? Banks also try to evade responsibility by saying, "We are not responsible." In this situation, will the government pay attention to this or not? To protect property or not? (Time expired.)
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota.
Honorable Ms. Samjhana Devkota (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, continuous rainfall from the 9th to the 11th has caused significant damage in Gorkha. In the mountainous district of Gorkha, the route from Chumanubri Rural Municipality and the Manaslu region towards Manang has been covered by snow, making it impossible to pass through Manang, leaving many tourists and local residents stranded. If the snow cannot be cleared, the residents of Samdo and Sama are facing starvation. Similarly, to go to Serab Gumba from Ward No. 4 of Lamobih, it takes a 4-hour trek through human settlements. There are about 500 people in Serab Gumba, Serab School, and Serab Old Age Home, and they have lost contact. There are more than 15 landslides, and it is said that it will cost more than 2 million rupees to clear the landslides. (Time expired.)
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Somnath Poudel.
Honorable Mr. Somnath Poudel (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, if someone asks why farmers cultivate crops, the answer would be to eat and support their families. However, for a long time, farmers in Jhapa have been forced to cultivate crops to feed wild elephants. In the current fiscal year, in Ward No. 7 of Kanchankawal Rural Municipality, Jhapa, elephants have damaged the paddy crops planted by farmers such as Tej Prasad Chamlagai, Chandrabahadur Limbu, Purnabahadur Phago, Vishnu Katwal, Anita Thapa, and Medini Khatiwada. Farmers in Jhapa have been suffering such damage for generations. When such damage occurs, the provision is to provide compensation of up to ten thousand rupees at a time. I demand that this compensation system, which provides only this much regardless of the extent of the damage, be immediately abolished, that attacks on humans by elephants be stopped, and that compensation be provided based on the extent of the damage. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, the order of speaking during the zero hour concludes here. Honorable members, names have been received on a party basis to speak during the special time. Now I will provide time for the honorable members to speak. First, Honorable Member Kiran Babu Shrestha, time 30 minutes. Following this, Honorable Member Suresh Kumar Ale Magar.
Honorable Mr. Kiran Babu Shrestha (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, in the past few years, many upheavals and accidents have occurred in the country. From 2007 BS to 2083 BS, accidents have severely affected the country. The country has suffered much loss and damage to life and property. In this context, some incidents were man-made, while some were natural. We may not have been able to prevent natural events, but we could have minimized them. However, we could have prevented man-made incidents or found solutions for them. Due to the failure to do so, the country has repeatedly fallen victim to such accidents and has been pushed back. Independent countries, countries that have progressed in democracy, whether we call it South Korea or India, have moved ahead in terms of development and have established themselves as developed nations, but we are still in a situation where in our villages and hilly regions, life is still lived relying on ropes and baskets.
Honorable Chairperson, in this context, the continuous rainfall from October 8th to 11th has caused floods, landslides, and inundation in various parts of the country. Especially in the Gandaki Province, the damage in districts like Baglung, Myagdi, Parbat, Mustang, Manang, and Tanahu has been extremely painful. According to preliminary reports, in Gandaki Province alone, 27 people have lost their lives, 9 have been injured, 19 citizens are missing, 2282 have been displaced, hundreds of houses are damaged or at high risk, and thousands of citizens are affected. Nine bridges, including suspension bridges, concrete bridges, and Bailey bridges, have been damaged by floods and landslides. Four have been completely damaged, and damage has been reported in 3 schools and 2 government offices. Landslides in the Thado River in Manang...

The incident of the river being blocked by a landslide had also made us more sensitive, but now we are hearing news that the danger has somewhat reduced as the water has started flowing slowly. Due to this flood and landslide, roads including the Kaligandaki corridor, Beni-Jomsom-Korla road, Besisahar-Manang road, and the Mid-Hill Highway within Gandaki Province have been completely obstructed. In this sad hour, I offer my heartfelt tribute to all the citizens who lost their lives in the floods and landslides. I express deep condolences to the bereaved families, wish for the speedy recovery of the injured, and urge the government to intensify the search for the missing citizens. This is not just an incident of a road collapsing, not just an incident of a bridge washing away, not just an incident of houses being submerged; it is an attack on the homes, livelihoods, hopes, and futures of the citizens. Gandaki is crying out for help today. Gandaki Province is not just a province of natural beauty; it is the backbone of Nepal's tourism. From the apples of Mustang to the agriculture of Myagdi, from the tourism of Manang to the economy of Pokhara, Gandaki is making a significant contribution to the country. It is also a context where Pokhara has been declared the tourism capital of Gandaki. But today, in some places in Gandaki, there are no roads, no bridges, no electricity, no communication, and no way to reach the market. In such a situation, a natural question arises: where is the federal government? What is the role of the provincial government? Where is the coordination with the local government? There was prior information, so where was the prior preparation? Honorable Chairperson, from October 9 to 11, the relevant bodies had already issued warnings about the possibility of heavy to very heavy rainfall in some places in Gandaki and Lumbini. They had also alerted about the risks of floods, landslides, and river erosion. Therefore, today my question is not just to assign blame, but how much prior preparation was there after receiving prior information? Were the risk-prone settlements identified? Were the citizens moved to safe places in time? Was there adequate emergency rescue equipment? Were helicopters, bulldozers, and rescue teams on standby in the remote districts? Will we become a state that only rushes after a disaster strikes, or a state that is prepared before the disaster strikes? I also demand and urge the government to declare Gandaki, like Bhote Koshi, as an area for rescue and relief. This should not be treated as a mere relief matter; all the mechanisms of the federal, provincial, and local levels should be operated through a single coordinated emergency mechanism. Immediate announcement of a special package for relief and rehabilitation for the families of the deceased, the injured, the displaced, and the homeless. Roads, bridges, electricity, and communication that are obstructed should be brought into operation immediately. The presence of the state in Gandaki should not be on paper but should be directly felt by the citizens. Just as Dashain is approaching, another big challenge has arrived there: the northern blockade. All the northern borders connected to Tibet are closed or obstructed due to the roads. There was only one Korala pass, and that too is now obstructed due to the road. Due to the obstruction of this pass with China, the supply of essential materials for our Dashain is being hampered due to the road. The closure of Tatopani, Rasuwagadhi, and Korala passes is greatly affecting the commercial supply system. We should not consider this as a mere commercial problem. It directly affects traders, indirectly affects consumers, and ultimately its burden reaches the kitchens of Nepali families. Goods are being held up due to the closure of the passes. Transportation costs have increased. Traders' investments are stuck. The supply of goods in the market is affected. The risk of price hikes during Dashain has also increased. Therefore, I have a clear question for the government. What alternative supply arrangements have been made? Where has the high-level dialogue with the Chinese government reached? When will Tatopani open? When will Rasuwagadhi and Kerung become operational? How quickly is Korala being made capable as an alternative pass? Traders have also urged the government to immediately talk with China, as the possibility of the Tatopani pass opening before Dashain is slim. The Gandaki disaster and the northern border obstruction have become a single national challenge. Honorable Chairperson, the Gandaki disaster and the northern border obstruction should not be viewed as separate problems. Both these issues are linked to Nepal's geographical sensitivity and infrastructural weaknesses. We built hilly and mountainous roads, but we did not build alternative roads along with them. We built bridges, but we did not arrange for an alternative route immediately after the bridge was washed away. We opened passes, but we did not build infrastructure so that another pass could bear the load if one closed. The definition of development must change now. Building a road is not just development; ensuring that the connection with citizens is not broken after the road is built is also development. Building a bridge is not just development; maintaining alternative connectivity after the bridge is built is development. Opening a pass is not just trade policy; developing a system that does not stop the country's supply even when the pass is closed, and building that, is a national strategy. Honorable Chairperson, I earnestly request the government that the country has suffered immense loss of life and property due to this flood and landslide, economically and socially. Therefore, it is necessary to quickly bring relief and supply packages, similar to past incidents, to the Gandaki province and other affected areas, to build bridges, and to reconnect the districts whose contact has been broken due to road blockages. Dashain is approaching. The roads to go home for Dashain are extremely risky. It is the government's responsibility to repair and construct these roads quickly. Although some of these roads fall within the provincial jurisdiction, they are under the federal government. I request that the federal government, in coordination with the province where it is feasible for the province, and with the federal government where it is not feasible for the province, should expedite the construction of these roads. Honorable Chairperson, regarding these incidents, I would now like to express my views on a slightly different matter. Honorable Chairperson, while entering into some contemporary issues, I would like to make a brief comment on the subject of Parliament today. Parliament is a forum to alert the government. This is the place where the voice of the people is raised through this sovereign parliament. Parliament is also a means to convey the problems of the people to the government and get them resolved. We brought this system of federal democratic republic, federal democratic republican system of governance, as stipulated in the constitution. Since then, the governments that have been in power in this manner have had great expectations from the people. When those expectations were not met, the people became dissatisfied. We said it repeatedly, standing in this parliament, we said it outside, we raised our voices. But because the people's expectations were not met, there have been repeated movements, repeated rebellions by the people. In the latest phase, the rebellion of the youth has brought a new kind of governance to this country. The system is the same, but a new governance has arrived. The governance is the same, but the face has changed. In the name of youth, with the hope and expectation that the youth will achieve something, the people have given their full support and formed this government. Looking at the government's activities for the past few months, have the works been done as the people expected? Has the pace of development progressed as the people expected? How much work has been done in the area of prosperity? Or, how successful has the current government been in reducing corruption, which has been vocal against corruption? These questions have arisen today. I think the work has not been done according to the people's expectations. Questions have also arisen as to whether this government can do it or not. Because, just as the morning indicates the day, the morning sun indicates the day, looking at the government's activities over the past 5-6 months, there is also very little room left to hope that it can do it now. In this context, today we have raised questions in Parliament, raised voices in Parliament. In a parliamentary system, Parliament is the supreme body. The government must be accountable to Parliament, and the government must answer the questions raised in Parliament. But we have raised issues repeatedly in the House of Representatives and the National Assembly, but the government does not seem to be listening. The government does not seem to be accountable to Parliament, and by circumventing the government, although such actions and incidents have happened in the past, the intention to rule through ordinances by bringing ordinances was seen yesterday as well, and it was a past weakness, we had raised our voice. The provision to bring ordinances in special circumstances, that provision, by disregarding it and acting according to one's own convenience, regardless of any difficult situation, the practice of running the government by bringing ordinances was done by past governments to some extent, and the current government, in the past days, we saw it tried to establish the practice of running the government through ordinances. We said this was a mistake in the past and it is a mistake now. If a government that is supposed to do good work follows such mistakes, but follows mistakes and weaknesses, then what is the change between the current government and the past government? What is the difference? Questions arise. Therefore, in the name of change, it is said that everything old was not good, the old made mistakes. Is it the government's job to just point out the mistakes of the past, or to do new work? There may be weaknesses, there may have been mistakes. But the government's responsibility is not fulfilled by just pointing out those mistakes, by showing those mistakes. What new work has the government done? What new change has the government brought? The people are evaluating, and will continue to evaluate, how much the government that came in the name of change has progressed in development work, how much it has progressed in prosperity. Perhaps the opportunity to do so in the future will be very limited. Because opportunities do not come all the time. If the opportunity that comes is not utilized properly, then nothing remains but regret later. In the past too, we saw that a government with nearly a two-thirds majority lost the opportunity it had to work. Even now, the government has a nearly two-thirds majority. I also request that this government, this majority government, should move forward without arrogance. The government is the executive, Parliament is the legislature and oversight body. The balance of power and parliamentary accountability strengthens democracy. Therefore, the government must be accountable to Parliament, and Parliament must be accountable to the people and the constitution. We are the opposition in this Parliament. The opposition is said to be the blind eye of the government. Therefore, the government should work to move forward by taking the voices raised by the opposition, not as an enemy, but as suggestions in the right way. And that is the core meaning of the parliamentary system. I have cited this example many times before: in Britain, the parliamentary government, the parliamentary system, the Prime Minister there pays more attention to the opposition than to his own wife, it is said. The government should work by paying more attention to what the opposition says, what it speaks, and what kind of reforms it brings.

It has been established. Therefore, the Prime Minister hesitates to come, the Prime Minister does not want to come here and answer, and the Prime Minister's inability to answer the representatives of the Parliament is not democratic accountability. We believed that we would build such a democracy. The Prime Minister and the ministers should stand up in Parliament and say, 'We are the government, therefore we have authority.' But we are the government of the people, therefore we are also accountable to Parliament. We need to have the courage to say that. We need to bring that into practice. I would also like to request the current government to do so. Another thing is that Parliament is not a rubber stamp for the government. The majority is currently with one party, almost two-thirds. We are seeing an environment in the House of Representatives where we just clap for whatever the government brings. Parliament should have the courage to stand up and say that what is wrong is wrong. But we clap for whatever the government brings. We have seen it, and it remains to be seen how right it is. We heard yesterday that we clapped even when the Prime Minister said something wrong. We heard applause even when it was said that we have encroached on India's land in this country. I think the public is watching today to see how right or wrong that was. Therefore, in a democracy, majority is the strength of the government. But majority is not a license to free the government from questioning. The majority can make laws, but it cannot go above the constitution. The majority can form a government, but it cannot suppress the voice of the people. Whether you like my views or not, I have the right to express my views, and that is the fundamental principle of democracy. We are expressing our views in this Parliament with necessity, and we should be allowed to express them, and if we do, that is also the practice of the parliamentary system. In a democracy, governance should not be based on the arbitrary whims of an individual, but on the rule of law. Therefore, I also request that the current government correct the issues raised about its working style and move forward. Today, the people want change, the people want development, the people want good governance, they want employment, they want to find a future in the country. With the formation of a strong and stable government, the people's hunger for development and prosperity has increased. However, the government's working style does not seem to be able to convey a positive message to the people as expected. The government's power should be used for public service, not to expand its influence. In a democracy, the government's evaluation should be based on results, not on propaganda. The people are asking. Where is the employment? Where is the employment? Where has production increased? Where is the policy to retain youth in the country? Where is good governance? When will the fruits of development reach the doorstep of the citizens? Therefore, Honorable Chairperson, may this not be considered mere criticism or commentary on the government, but rather a suggestion for improvement in the future. I have presented some suggestions and some views from the opposition. I also request that it be considered. Now we have come to this Parliament. We, the leaders and workers of all parties, have come forward to do politics. What is politics for? What is politics? I often see when I look around sometimes, and if a form comes, I see people writing 'politics' in the profession column. Is politics a profession? I don't think politics is a profession. I think politics is service, pure service, selfless service, and again service. If it were a profession, we could have done other jobs. I don't think most people come into politics by force or compulsion. I think we have entered politics for our own self-satisfaction, for the people, for public service, for the spirit of public service. We enter politics by embracing a principle, an ideology, and an ideal, and by being devoted to that principle, ideology, and ideal. Therefore, after entering politics and reaching power, the behavior and working style of those who do politics, the leaders and workers, is evaluated today, and it is a subject of evaluation among the public. There is a saying I heard. A person's life is influenced by three things! First, as a child, then as a youth, and then as an adult. That is about a person's youth. Another thing is that a person's face has three kinds of radiance: the first radiance is in the bright face of youth. It is smooth, rosy, and cannot be hidden! And as one gradually moves from youth to adulthood, the radiance of his face also fades. And the next radiance, the glow, comes when one has power. They call it the glow of power. When one has power, no matter how much one tries to hide their face, that radiance and glow come to the face, that glow of power attracts people. The cheeks are smooth, rosy, dressed accordingly, a bit suited and booted, up-to-date, and we have seen and experienced that when one has that power. And the next radiance and glow come when one has wealth. When one has abundant wealth, that glow of wealth cannot be hidden even if one tries to hide it! There is abundant wealth, but I don't have it, I am not doing anything, even then that glow of wealth brings radiance and glow to a person's face. Therefore, we have sometimes seen this kind of politics. But it is one thing to have that radiance. To become intoxicated in power, to become arrogant in power, to think that this country will always be mine is a shortcoming and a weakness, as we have seen in the past. Therefore, I think that in the future, those of us who are involved in politics, who have made many sacrifices in politics, perhaps fewer new youths have made them. Although we often hear about history, we have made many sacrifices for democracy. We have paid many prices. But some youths say, 'We were born later, what could we do?' If we had been born earlier, we would have made the same sacrifices. Although we have made many sacrifices, past sacrifices, past struggles, past democracy, this democracy, for the prosperity of this country, I request that we move forward without forgetting the sacrifices and history of our elders. Another most important thing in democracy is the rule of law. Finally, I want to say that this government should function according to the rule of law. There are rules, laws, and regulations, but if the government starts functioning in a monopolistic manner by violating laws and regulations, its lifespan will also be short, I think. Earlier, the Honorable Members raised questions during the zero hour. A few days ago, a person who had been the Chief Justice of this country, Cholendra Shumsher Rana, was arrested without any basis. He was taken into custody for 12 hours and then released. Under which law, under which rule was he apprehended? Under which crime was he apprehended? That remains unanswered to this day. The government has not spoken. Why was he arrested? Why was he apprehended? On what basis was a person who had even been the Chief Justice arrested? We have raised questions about these actions taken outside the law, and these questions are being raised in the market, and we are raising these questions in the House and Parliament to the government today. The government must answer. Cholendra Shumsher is just a representative example. Such incidents can happen in the future, and such incidents have happened in the past. The government apprehends, apprehends without basis, and the court releases. Therefore, whether to listen first and then apprehend, or to apprehend first and then listen, the government should be serious about this matter, and the public's trust should be carried forward by this government. The success of the government is the success of the people and the nation. We have no prejudice against the success of this government. But we want it to move forward in the right way. And finally, power is temporary, the government is temporary, the position is temporary, but the nation, the constitution, Parliament, and the sovereign rights of the people are permanent. Keeping this in mind, let this country move forward, and let us fulfill our responsibilities. With this, I conclude my remarks. Thank you, Jai Nepal. Presiding Officer: Honorable Vice-Chairperson Ms. Lila Kumari Bhandari. (14:08 hrs) Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Suresh Kumar Ale Magar, time (14:91 hrs) 14 minutes. After this, Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri. (Nepal Communist Party):- Honorable Mr. Suresh Kumar Ale Magar (14:92 hrs) Honorable Chairperson and all Honorable Members, I will also be standing at this rostrum for 14 minutes. You will have to tolerate me for these 14 minutes, for which I apologize. Honorable Chairperson, I want to talk about two disasters first. If time permits, I will discuss some other issues. Two disasters: one is natural disaster, a phenomenon created by nature, and the other is a phenomenon created by the government. Before the wounds caused by the devastating flood in Bhote Koshi could heal, Honorable Chairperson, on the 9th, 10th, and 11th of last month, a series of floods and landslides occurred across the country. This caused another disaster and devastation, and particularly in the districts of Manang, Myagdi, Baglung, Parbat, Palpa, etc., there was significant loss of life and property due to these floods and landslides. According to reports published in newspapers, 24 people have died, 14 are missing, 143 houses have been completely destroyed, and hundreds of families have been affected. Thus, this disaster has caused great damage to the Nepali people again. I want to express my heartfelt condolences to those who lost their lives in this disaster and wish a speedy recovery to the injured, and I want to state that the government should search for the missing persons immediately. Honorable Chairperson, many friends have already spoken about this. I also want to speak about it: Cholendra Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana, former Chief Justice. He was arrested from his residence at midnight on the 19th in a style of a raid, a dacoity. The government says he was not arrested, but we say it was an arrest. If he was arrested and taken away due to security reasons, due to a security threat, what kind of security is this? Honorable Chairperson, if someone is under a security threat, security personnel should be deployed at their home, not taken away. If this is a new way of providing security, then it is the government with a two-thirds majority's new way of providing security, wow! Honorable Chairperson, after being held in custody for 11 hours, he was released, but before that, during his custody, human rights commission officials went to meet him, but they were not allowed to meet him. If he was taken from his home due to a security threat, why were they not allowed to meet him? This is our question. Firstly, he should not have been taken away like that, and if he was to be taken, he should have been allowed to meet them. Representatives of the National Human Rights Commission should have been allowed to meet him, but they were not. Therefore, we...

It seems, Dalme has some blackness. There was no other reason here, there was no security, this government is making excuses. Honorable Chairperson, when he was kept at the Teku Metropolitan Police Office's Crime Investigation Department, and not allowed to meet, and the people from the National Human Rights Commission were not allowed to meet, the National Human Rights Commission summoned the head of that office, SSP Santosh Man Shrestha, for a statement. Santosh Shrestha went to give his statement, and he has given a written statement. We want to know what that statement is. Honorable Chairperson, the National Human Rights Commission has not made this statement public. I want to demand that this statement be made public. Similarly, if it is permissible by the Honorable Chairperson and the honorable members, I want to say that this is also a demand of the National Assembly. The Nepali people, we, and this sovereign National Assembly have the right to know about the written statement given by SSP Santosh Shrestha, the chief of the Crime Investigation Department, Teku, to the National Human Rights Commission. Therefore, I want to strongly reiterate the demand that the statement, the written statement, be made public. Honorable Chairperson, although Cholendra Shumsher J.B.R. is not a person who has bathed in milk, his various judgments as a judge at different levels are controversial. Similarly, he has been acquitted in major cases. To the extent that even the judges of the Supreme Court went on strike against him when he was the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the Nepal Bar Association boycotted his benches. To mitigate this, we need to raise awareness. That is one aspect. Another aspect is that human-wildlife conflict does not follow a single pattern. We implement a rule to drive away monkeys for some time, and after they follow it, it doesn't work again. Thus, we need to adopt various methods, and for that, our experts are also conducting studies and research. The Ministry of Science and Technology is also working on this. sections.summary_en: The National Assembly meeting commenced at 1:31 PM under the chairmanship of Narayan Prasad Dahal. The chairperson announced the commencement of the proceedings and called for the first speaker during the zero hour.

sections.name: Zero Hour
sections.summary_en: Several members raised concerns during the zero hour. Topics included the midnight arrest of the former Chief Justice, infrastructure issues like roads and bridges in various regions, embankment safety, the impact of natural disasters, price hikes, and digital security concerns. Members demanded government responses and actions.

sections.name: Special Time
sections.summary_en: The session moved to 'Special Time' with Honorable Member Kiran Babu Shrestha speaking first. He discussed the country's historical upheavals, comparing Nepal's development to other nations and highlighting the impact of both man-made and natural disasters, particularly the recent floods and landslides in Gandaki Province.

speakers.name: Kiran Babu Shrestha
speakers.topic: Country's upheavals, development comparison, disaster impact

sections.name: Opening
sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses the impact of recent floods and landslides in Gandaki Province, highlighting the obstruction of major roads and the need for government intervention. They also raise concerns about the preparedness for natural disasters and the effectiveness of the current government's actions.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Opening remarks and discussion on Gandaki disaster

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker details the severe damage caused by floods and landslides in Gandaki Province, including road blockages and the disruption of essential services. They urge the government to provide immediate relief, rehabilitation, and to declare the affected area as a rescue and relief zone. The speaker also addresses the issue of the northern border blockade, its impact on trade and supply, and questions the government's preparedness and diplomatic efforts.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Gandaki disaster and northern border blockade

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker argues that the Gandaki disaster and the northern border blockade are interconnected issues highlighting Nepal's geographical vulnerabilities and infrastructural weaknesses. They call for a redefinition of development to include ensuring continuous connectivity and robust supply systems, not just building infrastructure.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Interconnectedness of Gandaki disaster and border blockade

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker reiterates the urgent need for relief and rehabilitation packages for the Gandaki region, emphasizing the repair of roads and bridges before the upcoming Dashain festival. They call for coordinated efforts between federal and provincial governments to address these issues.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Urgent relief and rehabilitation for Gandaki region

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker shifts focus to the role of Parliament and government accountability, criticizing the current government's performance and lack of responsiveness to parliamentary concerns. They question the government's effectiveness in development and corruption control, drawing parallels with past governments and warning against arrogance.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Government accountability and parliamentary role

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker criticizes the government's tendency to bypass Parliament by using ordinances and urges them to heed the opposition's suggestions, emphasizing the importance of constructive dialogue and the core principles of a parliamentary system.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Criticism of ordinances and importance of opposition

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker criticizes the government's lack of accountability to Parliament, its perceived use of Parliament as a rubber stamp, and its failure to deliver on public expectations for development and good governance. The speaker emphasizes that democracy requires adherence to the rule of law and that the government's actions, such as the arrest of the former Chief Justice, are outside legal boundaries. The speaker also reflects on the nature of politics as service rather than a profession and the importance of remembering past sacrifices for democracy.

speakers.name: Suresh Kumar Ale Magar
speakers.topic: Government accountability, rule of law, nature of politics

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses two types of disasters: natural and government-induced. They highlight the recent floods and landslides causing significant damage and loss of life, expressing condolences and urging the government to search for the missing. The speaker reiterates concerns about the arrest of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana, questioning the legality and transparency of the action and the denial of access to human rights officials.

speakers.name: Ram Kumari Jhankri
speakers.topic: Disasters, former Chief Justice arrest, human rights

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: A member raised concerns about the government making excuses regarding security and demanded transparency regarding a written statement given to the National Human Rights Commission by SSP Santosh Man Shrestha. Another member discussed the controversial past of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher J.B.R. and warned against authoritarian tendencies. The discussion also touched upon the Prime Minister's UN address, climate change, and the suspension of ANFA by FIFA due to government interference.

They urged the government to focus beyond immediate relief to long-term rehabilitation, including search for the missing, safe housing, and livelihood restoration, emphasizing the needs of vulnerable groups.

sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses the need for comprehensive rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts following floods, emphasizing self-reliance for citizens and a national action plan for rebuilding infrastructure. The speaker also highlights discrepancies in data regarding missing persons and criticizes the government's approach to disaster management and civil service reform.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Ghanshyam Rizal raised concerns about the government's lack of responsiveness to public issues, including soaring ghee prices, long gas queues, and the plight of squatters. He criticized the government's performance over the past 182 days and questioned its commitment to development and good governance. He also highlighted issues like diplomatic weaknesses, the use of ordinances, and the treatment of journalists and former officials. The speaker concluded by urging the government to be accountable and deliver results, warning of public dissatisfaction in future elections.

speakers.name: Ghanshyam Rizal
speakers.topic: Government accountability, public issues, development, and governance

sections.name: Questions
sections.summary_en: The session transitioned to ministry-wise questions and answers. Honorable Member Rukmini Koirala asked the Minister of Agriculture, Forest and Environment about the government's measures to address crop damage by wild animals and provide compensation to farmers. Minister Gita Chaudhary responded by outlining the government's priority on human-wildlife conflict mitigation, including compensation, early warning systems, and the "Managed Human-Tiger Interface Project."

The Minister of Agriculture, Forest, and Environment addressed concerns about the effectiveness of current programs and assured that legal amendments are underway.
